quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on how warp breaks are expressed fairly and what happens to the count when yarn is sized.

questions.q: Why is 'one break every 51 lb' a poor way to compare warps of different counts?
options: Because breaks are counted on the loom, not the warper
Because 51 lb of a fine yarn is a much longer length than 51 lb of a coarse yarn
Because pounds are not a metric unit
Because the size add-on changes the weight
questions.explain: Fifty-one pounds of Ne 60 contains nearly three times the yardage of 51 lb of Ne 21, so a break per 51 lb is a far better performance for the finer yarn. Length, not weight, is the fair base.

questions.q: The standard unit the lecture uses to compare breakage rates between mills is:
options: Breaks per 10 million metres of yarn
questions.explain: Breaks per 10⁷ m removes the effect of count and lot size, so a warper on Ne 21 and a sizer on Ne 60 can be compared directly.

questions.q: The lecture states that quoting breaks per pound flatters coarse yarns.
questions.explain: A pound of coarse yarn is a short length, so fewer breaks per pound are recorded even if the yarn breaks just as often per metre. The Ne 21 warp at 51 lb per break is actually the worse performer.

questions.q: Which of the two warps in the lecture performs better: Ne 21 breaking every 51 lb or Ne 60 breaking every 27 lb?
options: Ne 21, because 51 lb is more than 27 lb
Ne 60, because its breaks per 10 million metres are lower (about 8 against 12)
questions.explain: Converted to length, Ne 60 runs about 1.24 million metres between breaks against about 0.82 million for Ne 21, so Ne 60 has about 8 breaks per 10⁷ m and Ne 21 about 12.

questions.q: What does 'size add-on' mean?
options: The extra length of warp allowed for sizing waste
The weight of size on the yarn as a fraction of the unsized yarn weight
The number of extra ends added for the selvedge
The increase in yarn diameter after sizing
questions.explain: A 12.5 % add-on means the sized warp weighs 1.125 times the unsized warp: 1,446.4 lb becomes 1,627.2 lb.

questions.q: After sizing, the yarn is described as 'coarser'. Why?
options: Because the yarn is stretched and becomes longer
Because size adds weight but no length, so there are fewer yards per pound
Because sized yarn is twisted harder
Because the fibres swell in water
questions.explain: Count in Ne is yards per pound ÷ 840. The size adds weight without adding length, so yards per pound fall and the Ne number drops from 20 to 17.8.

questions.q: Sized count is higher than the unsized count because the yarn has gained weight.
questions.explain: Ne is an indirect count: heavier yarn per yard means a LOWER number. Sized count = Ne ÷ (1 + add-on) = 20 ÷ 1.125 = 17.8.

questions.q: The lecture gives two uses for the sized count. Which pair is correct?
options: Loom-side yarn stock calculations and weight-based selling of fabric
Setting loom speed and reed count
Choosing cone size and creel capacity
questions.explain: Yarn stock at the loom is weighed in its sized state, and when fabric is sold by weight the size on the warp is part of that weight, so the sized count is needed for both.

questions.q: In the breakage worksheet, 'm per break' is obtained from 'yd per break' by:
questions.explain: A yard is shorter than a metre, so yards ÷ 1.0936 = metres (equivalently × 0.9144); 902,110 yd becomes 824,899 m.

questions.q: A lower figure for breaks per 10 million metres means:
options: Better performance: fewer stops per length run
questions.explain: The figure counts stoppages per fixed length of yarn; fewer breaks per 10⁷ m means the warp runs longer between stops, which is better regardless of count.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The conversion chain from pounds per break to breaks per 10 million metres, and the sized-count relation.

questions.q: Yards per break equals:
questions.explain: Each pound of Ne yarn is 840 × Ne yards, so the yards run between breaks are lb per break × 840 × Ne: 60 × 27 × 840 = 1,360,800 yd.

questions.q: Breaks per 10 million metres equals:
questions.explain: If one break occurs every 1,244,331 m, then in 10,000,000 m there are 10⁷ ÷ 1,244,331 = 8.04 breaks.

questions.q: With the same pounds per break, moving from Ne 20 to Ne 40 makes the breaks per 10 million metres:
questions.explain: Twice the count means twice the yards (and metres) per break, so half as many breaks per fixed length.

questions.q: Sized count equals:
questions.explain: Weight rises by the factor (1 + add-on) while length is unchanged, so Ne (an indirect count) is divided by that factor: 20 ÷ 1.125 = 17.8. Multiplying would wrongly make the yarn finer.

questions.q: Sized warp weight = unsized warp weight × (1 + size add-on).
questions.explain: The add-on is a fraction of the unsized weight, so 1,446.4 lb × 1.125 = 1,627.2 lb at 12.5 % add-on.

questions.q: Unsized warp weight on a beam is calculated as:
questions.explain: Total yarn length = ends × beam length; dividing by yards per pound (840 × Ne) gives pounds.

questions.q: If the size add-on rises from 10 % to 20 % on an Ne 20 warp, the sized count:
questions.explain: 20 ÷ 1.10 = 18.2 and 20 ÷ 1.20 = 16.7; more size means a heavier, coarser sized yarn.

questions.q: Because the size changes the count, the length of yarn on the beam also changes after sizing.
questions.explain: Size adds weight but no length; the yardage on the beam is the same before and after sizing, which is exactly why the count has to change.

questions.q: Which of the following would NOT change the breaks per 10 million metres figure for a warp?
options: Changing the lot from 1,000 lb to 2,000 lb with the same break frequency
questions.explain: The rate is per length, so the size of the lot does not matter; a bigger lot with the same breaks per pound gives the same rate. Count and lb per break both enter the formula directly.

questions.q: To convert a breakage rate from breaks per 10 million metres back to pounds per break for an Ne 20 yarn, you would:
options: Find metres per break = 10⁷ ÷ rate, convert to yards (× 1.0936), then divide by 840 × 20
questions.explain: Reverse the chain: metres per break = 10⁷ ÷ rate; yards = metres × 1.0936; pounds = yards ÷ (840 × Ne).

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Convert breakage reports into breaks per 10 million metres and work out sized weights and counts.

questions.q: A warper on Ne 30 reports one break every 40 lb. How many yards of yarn are run per break?
questions.explain: Yards per break = Ne × lb per break × 840 = 30 × 40 × 840 = 1,008,000 yd.

questions.q: Convert 1,008,000 yards per break to metres per break (to the nearest 100 m).
If one break occurs every 921,726 m, what is the breakage rate in breaks per 10 million metres (to two decimals)?
An Ne 60 warp breaks once every 27 lb. Find its breaks per 10 million metres (to two decimals).
A sizer on Ne 40 reports one break every 25 lb. Find the breaks per 10 million metres (to two decimals).
A beam carries 4,860 ends of Ne 20, each 5,000 yd long. What is the unsized warp weight in lb (to one decimal)?
An unsized warp of 1,446.4 lb is sized with a 12.5 % add-on. What does the sized warp weigh, in lb (to one decimal)?
questions.explain: Sized weight = 1,446.4 × 1.125 = 1,627.2 lb; the extra 180.8 lb is size.

questions.q: An Ne 20 warp receives 12.5 % size add-on. What is the count of the sized yarn (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: Sized count = 20 ÷ 1.125 = 17.78 Ne.

questions.q: An Ne 30 warp is sized with a 10 % add-on. What is the sized count (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: Sized count = 30 ÷ 1.10 = 27.27 Ne.

questions.q: An Ne 16 warp with a 15 % size add-on has a sized count closest to:
questions.explain: 16 ÷ 1.15 = 13.9. 18.4 is 16 × 1.15, the error of multiplying; 14.6 would be an add-on of about 10 %.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill-floor situations: reading breakage reports fairly, and using the sized count in stock and sales calculations.

questions.q: Two sizing machines report: machine X on Ne 21, one break per 51 lb; machine Y on Ne 60, one break per 27 lb. The sizing supervisor praises X. What should you tell him?
options: He is right; 51 lb per break is clearly better
Converted to length, Y has about 8 breaks per 10⁷ m and X about 12, so Y is performing better
The two cannot be compared because they run different counts
Both are equal when expressed per length
questions.explain: The lecture's point: 51 lb of Ne 21 is only about 0.82 million metres, whereas 27 lb of Ne 60 is 1.24 million metres. Counting per length, Y stops less often.

questions.q: A mill wants to set a target for warp breakage that applies to every count it runs. The target should be expressed as:
questions.explain: Only a per-length rate is independent of count, beam length and shift pattern, so one target can be used for Ne 10 and Ne 60 alike.

questions.q: Loom-side stock shows 500 lb of sized Ne 20 warp yarn (12.5 % add-on). To know how much actual yarn (without size) this is, the stock clerk should:
options: Leave it at 500 lb; size does not count
questions.explain: Sized weight = unsized × 1.125, so unsized = 500 ÷ 1.125 = 444 lb of yarn, with 56 lb of size on it.

questions.q: Grey fabric is sold by weight. A costing clerk calculates the warp weight in the fabric from the unsized count Ne 20 although the warp is woven sized at 12.5 % add-on. The fabric weight will be:
options: Correct, since the count is the same yarn
Understated by about 11 % of the warp weight
questions.explain: The woven warp carries its size, so the real warp weight is 1.125 times the unsized figure; using Ne 20 misses the size and understates the warp by 1 − 1 ÷ 1.125 = 11 %.

questions.q: If a warper changes from Ne 21 to Ne 10 yarn and still reports one break every 51 lb, its breaks per 10 million metres have roughly doubled.
questions.explain: Ne 10 has less than half the yards per pound of Ne 21, so 51 lb is a much shorter length: 10 × 51 × 840 = 428,400 yd against 899,640 yd, and the rate per length rises from about 12 to about 26.

questions.q: A quality manager notices the sized beams weigh 10 % more than the unsized warper's beams that went into them. The size add-on is approximately:
questions.explain: Sized = unsized × (1 + add-on); a 10 % increase in weight means a 10 % add-on, and the sized count would be Ne ÷ 1.10.

questions.q: The sizing recipe is changed so that the add-on falls from 15 % to 10 % on an Ne 20 warp. For the loom-side stock calculation, the sized count used should change from:
questions.explain: 20 ÷ 1.15 = 17.4 and 20 ÷ 1.10 = 18.2; less size means a lighter, finer sized yarn.

questions.q: A warper reports 'one break every 51 lb' on Ne 21 for January and 'one break every 48 lb' on Ne 30 for February. Has performance improved?
options: No, 48 lb is less than 51 lb
Yes: 48 lb of Ne 30 is about 1.21 million yd per break against 0.90 million yd in January
No change, since both are around 50 lb
It cannot be judged without the beam length
questions.explain: 30 × 48 × 840 = 1,209,600 yd per break against 21 × 51 × 840 = 899,640 yd; per length, February has fewer breaks (about 9 per 10⁷ m against 12).

questions.q: Which figure in the sized-count worksheet does NOT change if the size add-on is altered?
options: Weight of size on the beam
questions.explain: Unsized warp weight depends only on ends, length and the original count. The add-on changes the sized weight, the sized count and the amount of size.

questions.q: A buyer complains that the delivered grey fabric weight includes size. From the mill's side, which statement is correct?
options: Size adds no weight, so the complaint is baseless
Size on the warp is real weight on the grey fabric; the agreed weight must say whether it is sized or desized
Size is removed on the loom
questions.explain: The lecture notes that the sized count is needed for weight-based selling of fabric: the size (12.5 % of the warp here) stays in the grey cloth until desizing, so contracts must state the basis.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems across breakage rates and sized counts, with the mistakes that most often spoil the answer.

questions.q: A warper runs Ne 24 at one break every 45 lb. Find the breaks per 10 million metres (to two decimals).
A mill sets a target of 8 breaks per 10 million metres. On Ne 20 yarn, how many pounds should run between breaks to meet it (to the nearest lb)?
questions.explain: Metres per break = 10⁷ ÷ 8 = 1,250,000 m = 1,367,000 yd; ÷ 16,800 yd/lb = 81 lb per break.

questions.q: A beam of 3,820 ends of Ne 20 carries 3,693 yd of warp. Find the sized warp weight at 12.5 % add-on, in lb (to the nearest lb).
A student writes: sized count = 20 × 1.125 = 22.5. The error and the correct answer are:
options: Should divide, giving 17.8, because heavier yarn has a lower Ne
questions.explain: Ne is indirect: adding weight without length lowers the count, so Ne ÷ 1.125 = 17.8. Multiplying gives a finer count, the opposite of what sizing does.

questions.q: A sized yarn tests at Ne 17.78. If the add-on was 12.5 %, what was the unsized count?
questions.explain: Unsized Ne = sized Ne × (1 + add-on) = 17.78 × 1.125 = 20.0.

questions.q: If both the count and the pounds per break double, the breaks per 10 million metres fall to one quarter.
questions.explain: Yards per break = Ne × lb × 840; doubling both multiplies the length per break by four, so the breaks per fixed length fall to a quarter.

questions.q: Which warp has the best breakage performance?
questions.explain: Yards per break: Ne 10 → 840,000; Ne 21 → 899,640; Ne 40 → 1,008,000; Ne 60 → 1,360,800. The longest run between breaks, Ne 60, has the lowest breaks per 10⁷ m even though its pounds per break are the smallest.

questions.q: Sized stock at the loom is 1,627.2 lb of Ne 17.78 (sized) yarn. How many yards of yarn is this (to the nearest 1,000 yd)?
questions.explain: Yards = lb × 840 × Ne = 1,627.2 × 840 × 17.78 = 24,303,000 yd, the same as the unsized 1,446.4 lb × 840 × 20, because sizing adds no length.

questions.q: A report says 'breaks per 10 million yards' instead of metres. Compared with the correct metric figure, the yard-based number is:
questions.explain: 10 million yards is a shorter length than 10 million metres (9.144 million m), so fewer breaks fall inside it: the figure is 1 ÷ 1.0936 = 0.914 of the metric rate, about 9 % lower.

questions.q: The warper is set to stop on every break and each stop costs 2 minutes. On an Ne 20 warp at 12 breaks per 10⁷ m, how much stop time does a 20,000,000 m run of yarn cause?
questions.explain: 20 million metres is 2 × 10⁷ m, so 24 breaks; at 2 minutes each that is 48 minutes of stop time.
